lesson.title: The Raw Material of Evolution: Variation Within Populations
lesson.summary: No two individuals in a population are genetically identical, and this variation, produced by mutation and by the reshuffling of alleles during sexual reproduction, is the raw material that natural selection acts on.
lesson.body:
Every individual in a population carries its own particular combination of alleles at each of its genes, its genotype, which interacts with the environment to help produce that individual's observable traits, its phenotype. Populations are almost never uniform. Individuals differ from one another, sometimes in obvious ways, such as height, coloration, or resistance to disease, and sometimes in ways detectable only by examining their DNA directly.

This variation comes from two main sources. The first is mutation, a change in the DNA sequence itself, which is the ultimate source of every new genetic variant that has ever existed. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but occasionally one turns out to be beneficial in a particular environment, and it is this trickle of new variation that keeps populations from ever running out of raw material over evolutionary time. The second source is genetic recombination during sexual reproduction, which does not create new alleles but reshuffles the ones already present into new combinations. During meiosis, crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, and the independent assortment of chromosomes further mixes maternal and paternal alleles, so that offspring routinely inherit combinations of alleles that neither parent had.

At any single gene, an individual's genotype can be homozygous, carrying two identical alleles, or heterozygous, carrying two different alleles. Looking across many genes at once, the overall level of heterozygosity in a population is itself a useful measure of how much genetic variation that population has to work with, populations with more heterozygosity generally have more raw material available for future change.

It is worth being clear about what variation alone can and cannot do. Variation is necessary for evolution, but it is not sufficient on its own. The next chapter asks how much of that variation is actually passed from parents to offspring, a question captured by heritability, and the chapter after that asks how the environment acts on heritable variation to drive natural selection.
